result: Conditional deletion of Robo3 in rhombomere 3 causes a partial crossing defect of trigemino-thalamic axons. In situ hybridization confirmed deletion of Robo3 expression in r3 at E12, and most GFP-labeled axons from the PrV failed to cross the midline, though some still crossed and all projected rostrally toward the forebrain.
evaluation: Claims C21-C29 provide converging evidence from in situ hybridization (C21), GFP tracing (C22, C26-C29), and quantitative analysis (C30-C31) demonstrating successful conditional knockout and partial crossing defect. The data are internally consistent and supported by appropriate controls (n=3/3).

result: Robo3 deletion did not alter development of the PrV nucleus, as evidenced by normal distribution of βgal+ neurons and organization of barrelettes.
evaluation: Claims C24-C25 are supported by histological data (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing normal barrelette organization and βgal+ neuron distribution. This control is important for establishing that the phenotype is specific to axon guidance rather than general developmental defects.

result: Ephrin-A5 expression gradients in the cortex and thalamus were unchanged in mutants, indicating that deletion of Robo3 in the brainstem did not affect expression of patterning cues in target regions.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are based on visual inspection of in situ hybridization with only n=2 samples and no quantification. While ephrin-A5 is one important patterning molecule, the authors do not examine other guidance cues. The sample size is insufficient for a definitive conclusion.

result: At P4, GFP+ axons from r3 had similar trajectories in the trigemino-thalamic tract in both control and mutant mice, projected to the dorsolateral VPM, and formed barreloids, though the tract appeared slightly more defasciculated in mutants.
evaluation: Claims C35-C38 are supported by 3D imaging data (iDISCO) with adequate sample size (n=5 for trajectory, n=14 for each genotype for VPM targeting). The observations are consistent across animals and documented in Figures 2A-B and Video 1.

result: The mutant VPM exhibits abnormal organization with two distinct domains: a lateral domain with high density of GFP+ axons and a medial domain with sparse GFP+ patches. Both domains contain barreloids of comparable surface area and are separated by a cytochrome oxidase-free septum.
evaluation: Claims C39-C45 are well-supported by cytochrome oxidase staining and GFP imaging (Figure 2B, n=4/4). Quantitative measurements show comparable areas (0.19±0.006 mm² vs 0.18±0.003 mm², p=0.46), and the septum is clearly visible in the data.

result: Anterograde tracing with carbocyanine dyes demonstrates that the mutant VPM receives bilateral innervation from the PrV, with the dense GFP+ lateral region corresponding to ipsilateral projections and the medial patches to contralateral projections.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 are supported by anterograde tracing data (Figure 2C). While C48-C49 are inferences, they are reasonable given the position, shape, and size of traced projections. The conclusion of segregated bilateral inputs (C50) follows logically from the data.

result: Retrograde tracing from the VPM labeled cell bodies in both ipsilateral and contralateral PrV nuclei in mutants (3.3 times more ipsilaterally), with neurons projecting to each side mixed in the ventral PrV.
evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by retrograde tracing data (Figure 2D, n=4/4) with quantification (n=3). The mixing of ipsilateral and contralateral projecting neurons in the PrV contrasts with their segregation in the VPM, which is an important observation.

result: A large fraction of rhombomere 3-derived trigemino-thalamic axons project ipsilaterally in mutants, though some still project contralaterally, possibly due to incomplete Cre recombination or crossing after recombination.
evaluation: Claim C54 is a reasonable inference from the tracing data. Claim C55 is speculative but acknowledges the incomplete penetrance documented in C30-C31 (88% recombination efficiency). The speculation is appropriately qualified and supported by the quantitative data.

result: At E15.5, ipsilateral and contralateral axons in the TT tract show a medial-to-lateral gradient organization, suggesting pre-sorting before reaching the VPM, but ipsilateral axons had no measurable temporal lead over contralateral axons.
evaluation: Claims C56-C57 are supported by developmental tracing data at E15.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, n=3). The observation that ipsilateral and contralateral axons are adjacent at the rostral-most sections argues against a temporal advantage for ipsilateral axons.

result: At E18, trigemino-thalamic axons have reached the VPM and terminals fill the whole dorsal region in both control and mutant embryos.
evaluation: Claim C58 is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B (n=3) and a citation to Kivrak and Erzurumlu, 2013. This establishes that both populations reach the target by E18.

result: ION lesion experiments demonstrate that both VPM domains in mutants contain functional whisker maps organized in rows. The GFP-dense lateral region receives ipsilateral inputs while the GFP-patched medial region receives contralateral inputs from the infraorbital nerve. Sensory deprivation causes the deprived map to shrink while the non-deprived map expands, indicating activity-based competition.
evaluation: Claims C59-C66 are well-supported by ION lesion experiments with appropriate controls (n=3 controls, n=5 mutants) and 3D imaging (Figure 3). The functional validation through lesions is critical for establishing that both domains represent genuine sensory maps. The competition result (C65-C66) is clearly demonstrated.

result: Whisker stimulation triggers c-Fos expression in both VPM maps in mutants, with bands of activity visible on different planes for ipsilateral versus contralateral representations, demonstrating that the barreloid organization is functional.
evaluation: Claims C67-C72 are supported by c-Fos immunolabeling after whisker stimulation (n=3, Figure 4B). The bilateral activation pattern in mutants contrasts with unilateral activation in controls, and the different spatial planes for ipsi/contra maps are clearly documented. The inference that the organization is functional (C72) is reasonable.

result: In the barrel cortex of mutants, barrels are more numerous (52±2 vs 33±0 in controls), smaller (0.04±0.01 mm² vs 0.09±0.02 mm², p<0.0001), and arranged into eight rather than five rows, with two separate cortical zones (central and peripheral) each containing distinct barrel rows. These abnormalities are consistent across hemispheres and ages (n=25/25).
evaluation: Claims C73-C77 are strongly supported by quantitative morphological data from Vglut2 and cytochrome oxidase staining (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplements 1-3). The large sample size (n=25/25) and statistical significance (p<0.0001) provide robust support. The consistency across ages and hemispheres strengthens the conclusion.

result: In mutants with unilateral whisker trimming, c-Fos is activated bilaterally in the PMBSF, with activation in peripheral barrel rows contralateral to intact whiskers and in central barrel rows ipsilateral to intact whiskers. Activation occurs across all cortical layers, demonstrating that crossed and uncrossed inputs are mapped as two segregated domains with the ipsilateral map nested within the contralateral map.
evaluation: Claims C78-C82 are well-supported by c-Fos activation experiments (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B). The bilateral activation pattern in mutants is clearly distinct from unilateral activation in controls. The observation of activation across all layers (C81) is important for establishing functional integration.

result: The two nested cortical maps have similar general orientation resembling controls, but show discontinuities in bilateral organization with clear separation of ipsi- and contralateral inputs. This suggests that nearest-neighbor interactions prevail over molecular pre-patterning to organize continuous peripheral representation, while molecular gradients maintain general map orientation.
evaluation: Claims C83-C87 represent the key mechanistic interpretation of the results. The observations (C83-C85) are supported by the c-Fos mapping data. The inferences about nearest-neighbor interactions versus molecular pre-patterning (C86-C87) are reasonable given the segregation of maps despite similar orientation, though they remain interpretations rather than direct demonstrations.

result: The total barrel map space is not increased in mutants (2.32±0.05 mm² in controls vs 1.90±0.12 mm² in mutants, p=0.04), and individual barrels are roughly half the size (44±2%) of controls, suggesting that ipsilateral and contralateral inputs compete for a defined cortical space.
evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by quantitative measurements with statistical analysis. The finding that total space is actually slightly decreased (p=0.04) while barrel number increases is important evidence for competition. The inference about competition (C89) is reasonable given these measurements.

result: ION lesion experiments in the cortex show that in mutants, barrels fuse in both ipsilateral and contralateral representations of the lesioned whisker pad, and the unlesioned representation expands at the expense of the fused map, demonstrating sensory activity-dependent competition for cortical space.
evaluation: Claims C91-C94 are supported by neonatal ION lesion experiments (Figure 6A, n=3/3 controls, n=5/5 mutants). The bilateral fusion in mutants contrasts with unilateral fusion in controls, and the expansion of the unlesioned map provides clear evidence for activity-dependent competition.

result: ClearMap analysis shows statistically significant differences in barrel cortex and VPM activity between shaved and stimulated sides that are opposite in controls versus mutants. The d row activity column registers in the same absolute brain position in both control and mutant ipsilateral maps.
evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by unbiased whole-brain ClearMap analysis (n=3 per group, Figure 7A). The registration of the d row in the same position (C96-C97) is an important observation suggesting that molecular pre-patterning constrains absolute position despite the aberrant ipsilateral projection.

result: In upper cortical layers 2-3, c-Fos activity expands between activated rows within each map but not across map boundaries, suggesting little to no direct horizontal integration between ipsilateral and contralateral whisker maps in upper layers.
evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are supported by layer-specific c-Fos analysis (Figure 7B, n=4) and citations to prior work on cortical integration. The observation that expansion respects map boundaries is clear in the data. The inference about lack of integration (C100) is reasonable but could benefit from additional functional tests.

result: Uncrossing trigemino-thalamic axons results in duplication of facial whisker representation with two segregated maps sharing the same cortical space. Rather than forming an interspersed 'biwhisker' representation as predicted by point-to-point molecular guidance, complete segregation was observed with each map following spatial continuity of whisker inputs while retaining correct orientation and topography. This demonstrates that genetic pre-patterning and preservation of input continuity interact to control position and layout of somatosensory maps.
evaluation: Claims C101-C105 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing results from multiple experiments. The observations (C101, C103-C104) are well-supported by the data. The contrast with the alternative hypothesis (C102) strengthens the argument. The mechanistic conclusion (C105) is a reasonable inference from the totality of the data.

result: The absence of left-right mixing in the mutant somatosensory cortex differs from the binocular visual cortex, suggesting that mechanisms for bilateral integration present in the visual system may be absent from the somatosensory system, potentially representing evolutionary mechanisms governing sensory information processing.
evaluation: Claims C106, C111, C113 are supported by comparison with visual cortex organization (citation to Sato and Stryker, 2008). Claim C114 is more speculative but appropriately qualified. The comparison is valid and highlights an important difference between sensory systems, though the evolutionary interpretation remains hypothetical.

result: Previous studies using the same conditional Robo3 mutant in olivo-cerebellar and auditory systems found that affecting laterality did not affect topographic targeting, though synaptic maturation was delayed in the calyx of Held.
evaluation: Claims C107-C110 accurately summarize prior work (citations to Badura et al., 2013 and Michalski et al., 2013). This contextualizes the current findings within the broader literature on Robo3 function in different neural systems.

result: The somatosensory system combines two mapping rules: continuous topographic representation of the body surface and organization into distinct functional units.
evaluation: Claim C112 is a reasonable inference from the observed organization of the whisker maps, which show both continuous topography within each map and discrete functional units (barrels/barreloids). This interpretation is consistent with established understanding of somatosensory organization.

result: The orientation of the two whisker maps was similar in rostrocaudal and mediolateral axes, indicating that matching gradients of guidance molecules and their receptors were unchanged, which was confirmed for ephrin-A5.
evaluation: Claim C115 is supported by observation of map orientation. However, claim C116 relies on limited ephrin-A5 data (n=2) without quantification. While the inference is reasonable, the evidence for unchanged molecular gradients is insufficient. Additional guidance molecules should be examined.

result: The normal orientation of the ipsilateral map despite switched laterality could result from either torsion of the ascending tract en route to the VPM or correction at the target site through Eph/ephrin gradients, potentially involving axonal pruning and refinement mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C117-C120 are entirely speculative (all marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type). While the hypotheses are plausible and cite relevant prior work, no experimental data are provided to test these mechanisms. These remain open questions requiring future investigation.

result: The results illustrate the remarkable plasticity of the mammalian brain and its ability to accommodate changes in afferent wiring to create new maps and bilateral representations, and to compensate for major axon guidance defects in developmental brain disorders.
evaluation: Claims C121-C123 represent appropriate concluding statements. C121 is established knowledge. C122-C123 are reasonable inferences from the experimental results, supported by citations to relevant clinical literature (Jen et al., 2004; Muckli et al., 2009; Williams et al., 1994). The conclusions are appropriately qualified.

result: Robo3 is transiently expressed in r3 neurons during development, with expression stopping shortly after axon crossing, suggesting it does not play a role in later developmental stages such as axon targeting.
evaluation: Claims C124-C125 are supported by citations to prior work (Badura et al., 2013; Michalski et al., 2013; Renier et al., 2010). This temporal expression pattern is important for interpreting the specificity of the phenotype to axon guidance rather than targeting.

result: In adult heterozygous mice, 88% of NeuN+ neurons in ventral PrV express βgal, while 10.7±1.5% do not and probably did not express Cre recombinase.
evaluation: Claims C30-C31 are supported by quantitative double-labeling data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, n=5). This quantification of recombination efficiency is important for interpreting the incomplete crossing phenotype and is appropriately acknowledged in the discussion.
